lineage_context.teaching_goal: Use opposite leaves, small 4-part flowers, an inferior 2-locular ovary and drupaceous fruit to define the dogwood branch of Cornales.

project_scope.note: The current pool contains Cornus drummondii, an accepted Texas-native species under current Kew.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: On a shrub/tree with opposite leaves, trace the lateral veins: dogwood veins commonly curve strongly toward the leaf tip. Then confirm clusters of small 4-part flowers above an inferior ovary and a fleshy drupe with a hard stone.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Trees or shrubs; project Cornus has opposite simple leaves, entire to weakly toothed margins, no obvious stipules, and strongly arcuate secondary veins.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Small flowers commonly 4-merous: 4 sepals, 4 petals and 4 stamens alternating with the petals. Ovary inferior, usually 2-locular with one ovule per locule.
family_diagnostics.fruit: A drupe, with persistent calyx/style remnants often visible at the apex; stone commonly 2-celled.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Opposite arcuate-veined leaves + tiny 4-part flowers + inferior ovary + drupe is the dogwood package.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: opposite arcuate leaf → 4-part flower → inferior ovary → drupe/stone → Hydrangeaceae comparison
visual_lesson.intro: Cornaceae is the small-flower, fleshy-fruit branch of this Cornales lesson.

steps.title: 1 · Trace the arcuate veins
steps.look_for: Strong lateral veins arching forward toward the tip instead of running straight to the margin.
steps.why_it_matters: It is a fast dogwood gestalt when combined with opposite leaves.

steps.title: 2 · Count four petals and four stamens
steps.look_for: Tiny 4-petaled flower with 4 stamens alternating with the petals.
steps.why_it_matters: This gives a clean contrast with Philadelphus's many-stamen flower.

steps.title: 3 · Confirm the inferior ovary
steps.look_for: Petals and stamens arise above the ovary; ovary usually has two locules with one ovule each.
steps.why_it_matters: Links the family to Cornales and predicts the drupaceous fruit.

steps.title: 4 · Open the drupe
steps.look_for: Fleshy outer fruit surrounding a hard stone, often with two internal chambers.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit is the easiest split from capsular Hydrangeaceae and Loasaceae.

comparisons.title: Cornaceae vs Hydrangeaceae
comparisons.rule: Both project families have opposite leaves and inferior ovaries. Cornus has tiny 4-part flowers with 4 stamens and a fleshy drupe; Philadelphus has 4 petals, many stamens and a dry many-seeded capsule.

comparisons.title: Cornaceae vs Viburnaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can be opposite-leaved woody plants with inferior ovaries and drupes. Use leaf venation, flower-cluster structure and stone/fruit details, then current family context.

comparisons.title: Cornaceae vs Loasaceae
comparisons.rule: Cornaceae is woody and drupaceous; Loasaceae is commonly rough/barbed/stinging and capsular with many stamens.

comparisons.title: Cornaceae vs Viburnaceae: count flower parts
comparisons.rule: Opposite leaves, arcuate venation and fleshy drupes can overlap. Typical Cornus flowers have four petals and four stamens; Viburnum generally has a five-lobed corolla and five stamens. Verify mature fruit/stone and genus characters; neither leaf arrangement nor arcuate veins alone proves family.

visual_lesson.caveat: Arcuate venation is a strong dogwood clue but not a stand-alone family character. Confirm the flower and fruit.

diagnostic_photo_needs.structure: opposite leaves with arcuate secondary veins

genera.fast_cue: opposite arcuate-veined leaves + tiny 4-part flowers + inferior ovary + drupe
